entries.question: How long was the Babylonian Captivity?
entries.summary: Jeremiah 25:11 and 29:10 set the Babylonian Captivity at seventy years. Baruch 6:2 — the Letter of Jeremiah — gives the duration as 'seven generations.' Even granting flexible generation-lengths, seventy years and seven generations are mathematically incompatible figures, and the historical-archaeological evidence makes both numbers schematic rather than literal.
entries.commentary:
Start with the actual historical chronology. The first Babylonian deportation under Nebuchadnezzar happened in 597 BCE; the destruction of the temple was 587/586 BCE; and the return under Cyrus's decree is conventionally dated to 538 BCE. So the captivity ran roughly 48 years from the destruction of the temple to the decree, or 59 years from the first deportation. Lester Grabbe in *A History of the Jews and Judaism in the Second Temple Period* does the math carefully and notes that the 'seventy years' of Jeremiah is already an approximation, not a hard count.

Where does the seventy come from? Jack Lundbom in the AB Jeremiah 21-36 documents the symbolic resonance: seventy is a round number in the Hebrew Bible (Israel's seventy nations, Moses's seventy elders, the seventy-week Daniel apocalypse), and it carries connotations of completion and divine ordering. The fact that the actual exile lasted roughly fifty years and Jeremiah rounds it to seventy is not a historical embarrassment — it's the prophet using a schematic number. William Holladay in the Hermeneia Jeremiah 1-25 reads the seventy-year figure as deliberate cosmological symbol, not chronicle.

Daniel 9 then extends and reinterprets Jeremiah's seventy years as seventy weeks of years, which is 490 years, which gets you from the exile down to the Maccabean crisis. John Collins in the Hermeneia Daniel makes the case decisively: Daniel 9 is a second-century BCE apocalyptic recalculation of an already-schematic Jeremianic number. So even within the Jewish canon, the seventy-year duration is being treated flexibly.

Baruch's Letter of Jeremiah (deuterocanonical Baruch 6, in the Vulgate's numbering — what Greek MSS call the Epistle of Jeremiah) sets the duration at seven generations. Carey A. Moore in the AB volume on Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah dates the work to roughly the late fourth or third century BCE and notes that 'seven generations' is itself a schematic figure derived from Genesis-style genealogical theology — seven is the perfection-number. A biblical generation is usually reckoned at 30-40 years, which gives a range of 210-280 years. That's not 70 years.

The apologist harmonization runs through several paths. Path one: maybe Baruch is talking about something different — a longer cultural exile rather than the strict political one. Path two: 'seven generations' is loose figurative language. Path three: the Letter of Jeremiah isn't canonical anyway (Protestant move), so the contradiction doesn't matter. All three moves have some traction, but they don't dissolve the underlying issue, which is that Second Temple Jewish literature contained multiple, incompatible schematizations of how long the exile was. Jeremiah says seventy years. Daniel says seventy weeks of years. Baruch says seven generations. Critical chronology says about fifty years from temple destruction to return. Lester Grabbe's bottom line is that the duration of the Babylonian Captivity was a theological construct first and a chronological measurement second, and the biblical witnesses themselves can't agree on the number. Take your pick — and notice that no historical reading lands you at 70 exact years anyway.

answers.answer_explanation:
And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years. Jeremiah 25:11

Thus saith the LORD, That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place. Jeremiah 29:10
When you are come into Babylon, you shall be there many years, and for a long time, even to seven generations. Baruch 6:2

commentary_out.commentary:
The historical chronology should anchor the discussion. The first Babylonian deportation under Nebuchadnezzar occurred in 597 BCE; the destruction of the temple followed in 587/586 BCE; the return under Cyrus's decree is conventionally dated to 538 BCE. That yields roughly 48 years from the temple's destruction to the decree, or about 59 years from the first deportation — in neither case a literal seventy. Lester Grabbe, in his history of the Persian-period province of Yehud, works the arithmetic and treats Jeremiah's 'seventy years' as an approximation and theological construct rather than a hard count, and Rainer Albertz's study of the exile reaches a similar conclusion about the schematic character of the figure.

The origin of the seventy is symbolic. Jack Lundbom, in the Anchor Bible Jeremiah 21-36, documents the resonance of seventy as a round number of completion in the Hebrew Bible — the seventy nations of Genesis 10, the seventy elders of Exodus 24, the seventy years of a human lifespan in Psalm 90:10. A Babylonian parallel reinforces the point: an inscription of Esarhaddon assigns Babylon itself a seventy-year period of divine abandonment, a near-formulaic span for a deity's withdrawal. William Holladay, in the Hermeneia Jeremiah, reads the seventy-year figure as deliberate symbol rather than chronicle. That the actual exile ran roughly half a century while the prophet rounds it to seventy is not a historical embarrassment but a feature of schematic prophecy. Daniel 9 confirms the figure's elasticity within the canon itself: it reinterprets Jeremiah's seventy years as seventy weeks of years — 490 years — stretching the prophecy down to the Maccabean crisis. John Collins, in the Hermeneia Daniel, shows this to be a second-century BCE apocalyptic recalculation of an already-schematic number. 2 Chronicles 36:21 offers yet another rationale, tying the seventy years to the land's missed sabbatical rests.

The Epistle of Jeremiah — transmitted in Greek manuscripts and appearing as Baruch 6 in the Vulgate's numbering — gives the duration as 'seven generations.' Carey Moore, in the Anchor Bible volume on the additions, dates the work to roughly the late fourth or third century BCE and identifies 'seven generations' as itself a schematic figure rooted in genealogical perfection-theology, seven being the completeness-number. A biblical generation is conventionally reckoned at thirty to forty years, yielding a span of 210 to 280 years — manifestly not seventy.

The apologetic case runs along three paths. First, the Epistle may envision a longer cultural or religious exile rather than the strict political captivity, so the two are not measuring the same thing. Second, 'seven generations' is loose figurative idiom for 'a long time,' as the verse's own framing ('many years, and for a long time') suggests. Third, on the Protestant canon the Epistle of Jeremiah is non-canonical, so no intra-scriptural contradiction arises at all. Each path has genuine traction, and together they substantially defuse the charge: both numbers are best read as theological schemata, not arithmetic, and they were never intended as competing stopwatch readings. Yet the reconciliation is only partial. The deeper datum survives every harmonization: Second Temple Jewish literature preserved multiple, mutually incompatible schematizations of the exile's length — seventy years (Jeremiah), seventy weeks of years (Daniel), seven generations (Epistle of Jeremiah) — none of which matches the historical span of roughly fifty years from the temple's fall to the return. Grabbe's bottom line stands: the duration of the captivity was a theological construct before it was a measurement, and the witnesses do not agree. Verdict: harmonizable as competing schematic symbols (and moot on the Protestant canon), but historically none of the figures is literal.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: Both figures are recognized as schematic theological numbers rather than literal chronological counts (seventy = completeness; seven generations = perfection), so they are not competing arithmetic measurements of the same span; on the Protestant canon, Baruch/Epistle of Jeremiah is non-canonical, removing the conflict entirely. The reconciliation is partial because Second Temple literature still contained multiple incompatible schematizations and neither figure matches the actual ~50-year span.

entries.question: Will Ephraim return to Egypt?
entries.summary: Hosea 8:13 and 9:3 announce that Ephraim — the northern kingdom — will return to Egypt as punishment. Hosea 11:5 declares that Ephraim shall not return into the land of Egypt, but rather the Assyrian will be his king. The contradiction is internal to a single prophet, and the prophet doesn't seem to notice the problem.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleaner intra-book contradictions in the prophetic literature. Two declarations, three chapters apart, both attributed to the prophet Hosea, both about the same nation, both predicting opposite outcomes. Hosea 8:13 — mitsrayim yashuvu, 'to Egypt they shall return' — and 9:3 — Ephraim shall return to Egypt and eat unclean things in Assyria — versus 11:5 — lo' yashuv el-erets mitsrayim, 'he shall not return to the land of Egypt,' but Assyria shall be his king.

The critical commentators have generally taken one of three approaches. Approach one: the verses come from different compositional layers, and the contradiction reflects different prophetic moments preserved in the redacted book. Hans Walter Wolff in the Hermeneia Hosea reads 8:13/9:3 as early Hosean material from the period before the Assyrian deportation, when 'return to Egypt' was still a live political possibility, and 11:5 as later material reflecting the actual Assyrian conquest. Approach two: 'Egypt' in Hosea is functioning as a theological symbol for slavery and judgment, not always a literal geographic destination. Francis Andersen and David Noel Freedman in the AB Hosea make a version of this case, reading 'return to Egypt' as a shorthand for reversal of the Exodus, with Assyria as the actual destination. Approach three: the verses are addressing different sub-groups within Ephraim, with some refugees fleeing to Egypt and others deported to Assyria. James Mays in the OTL Hosea entertains this option.

Each approach has some merit, but each comes at a cost. Approach one is the most historically respectable but concedes the contradiction is real — it just attributes it to redaction. Approach two requires reading 8:13 and 9:3 metaphorically while reading 11:5 literally, which is a directionality the text doesn't signal. Approach three has slight historical support — Jeremiah 41-44 records actual Judean refugees fleeing to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem, and there's no reason a similar thing couldn't have happened with northerners — but the verses themselves don't make that subgroup distinction.

The simplest critical reading is Wolff's redaction-history one. The book of Hosea was composed across decades during the lead-up to and aftermath of the Assyrian destruction of the northern kingdom in 722 BCE, and the prophet's predictions about Egypt got modified as actual political events unfolded. The 'will Ephraim return to Egypt' question doesn't have a single answer in Hosea because the book is a compilation of oracles delivered at different historical moments under different political assumptions. The contradiction is genuine, and trying to harmonize it without acknowledging compositional history requires you to allegorize verses the prophet probably meant literally.

answers.answer_explanation: Ephraim ... shall return to Egypt. Hosea 8:11-13, 9:3
Ephraim ... shall not return into the land of Egypt. Hosea 11:3-5

commentary_out.commentary:
This is among the cleaner intra-book contradictions in the prophetic literature: two declarations three chapters apart, both attributed to Hosea, both concerning the same nation (Ephraim/the northern kingdom), predicting opposite outcomes. Hosea 8:13 reads hēmmâ mitsrayim yashuvu — 'they shall return to Egypt' — and 9:3 sharpens it: Ephraim shall return to Egypt and in Assyria eat unclean food. Against these stands 11:5: lo' yashuv 'el-'erets mitsrayim — 'he shall not return to the land of Egypt,' but Assyria shall be his king. The same verb (shuv, 'return') and the same destination (Egypt) are affirmed and denied within a single short book.

A textual wrinkle deserves note. The Masoretic Text of 11:5 begins with lo' ('not'), but the standard LXX-influenced emendation (followed by RSV/NRSV and surveyed by Macintosh in the ICC) moves that negative particle back to the end of the immediately preceding verse, 11:4, re-pointing it as לוֹ (lô, 'to him') — an object marker for the verb in 11:4 rather than a negation in 11:5. Strip the lo' out of 11:5 and the verse reads 'he shall return to the land of Egypt,' which now agrees with 8:13 and 9:3. The Septuagint reflects exactly this uncertainty. Adopt the emendation and 11:5 harmonizes with the earlier oracles — but it does so by textual surgery, not exegesis, and the MT as transmitted plainly contradicts them. Macintosh, in the International Critical Commentary Hosea, surveys the variants and the difficulty of the verse.

Critical commentators have taken three main approaches. First, redaction history: the verses derive from different compositional moments preserved in the edited book. Hans Walter Wolff, in the Hermeneia Hosea, reads 8:13 and 9:3 as earlier Hosean material from a period when flight to Egypt was a live political option (Israel did at times seek Egyptian alliance against Assyria, cf. Hos 7:11; 12:1), and 11:5 as reflecting the actual outcome — Assyrian deportation following the fall of Samaria in 722 BCE. Second, the symbolic reading: 'Egypt' functions as a theological cipher for bondage and the reversal of the Exodus rather than a literal destination. Francis Andersen and David Noel Freedman, in the Anchor Bible Hosea, develop this, taking 'return to Egypt' as shorthand for un-doing the Exodus, with Assyria the literal destination. Third, the subgroup reading: different segments of Ephraim meet different fates, some fleeing to Egypt and others deported to Assyria. James Mays, in the Old Testament Library Hosea, entertains this, and it has a historical analogue — Jeremiah 41-44 records Judean refugees fleeing to Egypt after Jerusalem's fall, so a comparable northern flight is not implausible.

Each approach carries a cost. The redactional reading is the most historically defensible but explicitly concedes that the contradiction is real, locating it in the book's composition rather than dissolving it. The symbolic reading requires construing 8:13 and 9:3 metaphorically while reading 11:5 literally — an asymmetry of interpretation the text gives no signal to license; if 'Egypt' is figurative in 8:13, consistency would make it figurative in 11:5 too, and the contradiction returns at the level of whether the figure applies. The subgroup reading has the most surface plausibility but is not what the verses say: neither passage distinguishes refugees from deportees, and 11:5 flatly denies the Egypt-return that 9:3 just affirmed of the same 'Ephraim.' The simplest critical account remains Wolff's. The book of Hosea was assembled across decades spanning the lead-up to and aftermath of the Assyrian destruction of the northern kingdom, and oracles delivered under shifting political assumptions were preserved side by side without harmonization. The question 'will Ephraim return to Egypt?' has no single answer in Hosea because the book is a compilation, not a unified prediction. The contradiction is genuine; the only harmonization that does not require allegorizing verses the prophet likely meant literally is to relocate the tension into the book's redactional history — which is to grant the contradiction at the level of original composition. Verdict: genuine internal contradiction, best explained by the book's compositional history.

issues.problem: The commentary describes the well-known textual emendation of Hosea 11:5 as attaching the negative particle lo' 'to the end of 10:15 instead (reading "in a storm... is cut off, no more").' The verse number is wrong. The standard LXX-influenced emendation (followed by RSV/NRSV and surveyed by Macintosh in the ICC) re-points/relocates lo' to the end of the IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING verse, Hosea 11:4 (read as לו, 'to him,' an object marker for the verb in 11:4), not to 10:15. The parenthetical gloss 'in a storm... is cut off, no more' actually describes the content of Hosea 10:15, compounding the conflation: the commentary has merged the content of 10:15 with the emendation target, which is 11:4. The broader point (MT has lo'; the emendation removes the negation and harmonizes 11:5 with 8:13/9:3) is sound, but a reader checking BHS or Macintosh would find the relocation target is 11:4, not 10:15. Verified against Macintosh ICC Hosea (1997) and the standard text-critical literature on Hos 11:4-5.
issues.correction: Change 'attach the negative particle to the end of 10:15 instead' to 'attach the negative particle to the end of the preceding verse, 11:4 (re-pointing it as לו, "to him")' and drop or relocate the '"in a storm... is cut off, no more"' gloss, which belongs to 10:15 and is not what the emendation produces. The resulting reading of 11:5 ('he shall return to the land of Egypt') is correctly stated.

entries.question: Did a fish or a whale swallow Jonah?
entries.summary: Jonah 1:17 (Hebrew 2:1) says YHWH appointed a dag gadol — a great fish — to swallow Jonah. Matthew 12:40 has Jesus refer to the same incident, but the Greek word used is kētos, traditionally rendered 'whale' in English versions following the KJV. The contradiction is partly a translation artifact (kētos is broader than the modern 'whale') but reflects a genuine LXX-to-NT terminological shift.
entries.commentary:
Start with the Hebrew. Jonah 1:17 (numbered Jonah 2:1 in the MT) reads vayman YHWH dag gadol livloa et-yonah — YHWH appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah. The word dag is the generic Hebrew word for fish, with no taxonomic precision. Jack Sasson in the AB Jonah notes that the Hebrew imagination didn't distinguish whales from large fish — cetaceans were just big fish — so dag gadol covers everything from a large tuna to a whale to a mythological sea-monster. The Hebrew is precise about size (gadol) and vague about species.

The Greek translators of the LXX rendered dag gadol as kētei megalō. The word kētos in Greek covers everything from large fish to whales to mythological sea-monsters — it's the word used for the sea-creatures in Homer and for the Greek Andromeda-rescue mythology. Aristotle uses kētos broadly. So kētos is etymologically and lexically the right Greek word for an unspecified large sea-creature. Matthew 12:40, when Jesus refers to the Jonah incident, picks up the LXX vocabulary directly: en tē koilia tou kētous — in the belly of the kētos.

The KJV translates kētos as 'whale.' That's a 1611 English translation choice based on the dominant Renaissance understanding of kētos as 'whale,' but it's not what kētos means lexically. Modern critical translations are split: the NRSV and NASB render Matthew 12:40 as 'sea monster,' the ESV and NIV as 'great fish' or 'huge fish,' while the NABRE retains the traditional 'whale.' Davies and Allison in the ICC Matthew acknowledge that the KJV rendering as 'whale' is misleading but note that the underlying Greek does not specify whale.

So the contradiction in its strong form — 'fish vs. whale' — dissolves into a translation issue. The KJV created the whale-vs-fish puzzle through anachronistic translation choices, and modern critical translations would render both passages with parallel vocabulary (large fish / sea-creature). The underlying Greek is not asserting whale-specifically.

But don't let the apologist celebrate too early. The harmonization saves Matthew 12:40 from a fish-vs-whale contradiction with Jonah 1:17 at the cost of conceding that the KJV — the translation that for four centuries shaped Anglophone Christian understanding of the text — was wrong about what Matthew said. And the deeper problem with Matthew 12:40 isn't the fish-vs-whale dispute; it's that the verse predicts Jesus will be 'three days and three nights' in the heart of the earth, while the Synoptic crucifixion-resurrection chronology has him buried Friday evening and rising Sunday morning — at most two nights and one full day. Dale Allison in *Resurrecting Jesus* documents this as one of the more genuinely difficult Synoptic chronology problems, and it's a problem this SAB entry doesn't even raise. The fish-vs-whale framing is mostly a KJV-translation artifact. The three-days-and-three-nights problem is real and unresolved.

answers.answer: Jonah was swallowed by a big fish.
answers.answer_explanation: Now the Lord had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. Jonah 1:17

answers.answer: Jonah was swallowed by a whale.
answers.answer_explanation: For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the whale's belly. Matthew 12:40

commentary_out.commentary:
Begin with the Hebrew. Jonah 1:17 (numbered 2:1 in the Masoretic Text) reads way-man YHWH dag gadol livloa' 'et-yonah — 'YHWH appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah.' The noun dag is the generic Hebrew word for fish, carrying no taxonomic precision; the text is specific about size (gadol, 'great') and indifferent about species. Jack Sasson, in the Anchor Bible Jonah, observes that the ancient Hebrew imagination did not separate whales from large fish — cetaceans were simply big fish — so dag gadol comfortably spans a large tuna, a whale, or a mythological sea-monster. James Limburg, in the Old Testament Library Jonah, makes the same point about the term's deliberate vagueness, which also evokes the chaos-monster imagery of texts like Job 7:12 and Psalm 74.

The Septuagint translators rendered dag gadol as kētei megalō. In Greek, kētos denotes any large sea-creature — it is the word Homer uses for the monsters of the deep, the term in the Andromeda-and-Perseus rescue myth, and a category Aristotle employs broadly in his zoology. Liddell-Scott-Jones glosses it as 'sea-monster, huge fish, whale.' It is, in short, the lexically appropriate Greek equivalent for an unspecified great sea-creature, not a technical term for the order Cetacea. Matthew 12:40, citing the Jonah episode, picks up the Septuagint vocabulary directly: en tē koilia tou kētous — 'in the belly of the kētos.' Matthew is quoting the Greek Jonah, not introducing a new zoological claim.

The famous 'whale' is a translation decision, not a feature of the text. The King James Version of 1611 rendered kētos as 'whale,' reflecting the dominant Renaissance understanding of the word, but this is narrower than the Greek warrants. Modern critical translations diverge accordingly: the NRSV and NASB render Matthew 12:40 as 'sea monster,' the ESV and NIV as 'great fish' or 'huge fish,' while the NABRE retains the traditional 'whale.' Davies and Allison, in the International Critical Commentary Matthew, note that the KJV 'whale' is misleading and that the underlying Greek specifies no such thing. The strong form of the alleged contradiction — 'fish versus whale' — therefore dissolves into a translation artifact manufactured by the KJV's anachronistic choice; rendered with parallel vocabulary, Jonah 1:17 and Matthew 12:40 say the same thing: a great fish / sea-creature.

The apologist is entitled to claim this harmonization, but at a price worth naming, and a deeper problem the SAB framing entirely misses. The price: the resolution concedes that the KJV — the translation that shaped four centuries of Anglophone Christian understanding — got the word wrong. The deeper problem: Matthew 12:40 has Jesus predict he will be 'three days and three nights' (treis hēmeras kai treis nyktas) in the heart of the earth, in explicit parallel to Jonah's three days and three nights in the fish. Yet the Synoptic passion chronology places the burial late Friday and the resurrection early Sunday — at most two nights (Friday, Saturday) and one full day, not three of each. Dale Allison, in Resurrecting Jesus, treats this as one of the genuinely difficult Synoptic chronology problems; the standard appeal to Jewish inclusive reckoning (any part of a day counting as a whole) can stretch 'three days' to cover Friday-Saturday-Sunday but cannot manufacture three nights from two. Proposed fixes — a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion to recover the missing night — conflict with the Gospels' own Passover-and-Sabbath sequence. The fish-versus-whale dispute is essentially a KJV-translation artifact and is rightly set aside; the three-days-and-three-nights tension is a real, unresolved problem the question does not even raise. Verdict: the fish/whale contradiction is harmonizable as a translation artifact; the underlying three-days-and-three-nights chronology is not.
commentary_out.harmonization_basis: The fish-vs-whale contradiction is a translation artifact: Hebrew dag gadol means 'great fish' generically and the LXX/Matthew kētos means 'large sea-creature/sea-monster,' not 'whale' specifically; the KJV's 'whale' is an anachronistic 1611 rendering. Modern critical translations render both passages with parallel vocabulary, dissolving the species conflict. The harmonization is only partial because Matthew 12:40 introduces a separate, unresolved 'three days and three nights' chronology problem.

entries.question: Did Jesus tell his apostles to go barefoot and without a staff?
entries.summary: Matthew 10:10 and Luke 9:3 / 10:4 record Jesus telling the disciples to take no staff and no shoes (sandals). Mark 6:8-9 records the opposite — "save a staff only" and "be shod with sandals." The same scene, the same instruction, three Synoptic Gospels and two incompatible packing lists.
entries.commentary: This is the textbook Synoptic-problem contradiction and it's one of the cleanest demonstrations that the gospel writers were freely editing their sources rather than reporting verbatim. Mark, the earliest, permits sandals and a staff. Matthew and Luke both prohibit both. The directionality matters: when Matthew and Luke independently agree against Mark, source critics look for a reason. The likeliest is that Matthew and Luke were tightening the instruction to match the more rigorous itinerant-prophet ideal already circulating in their communities (compare the Q Mission Discourse). The apologist harmonization, exhaustively cataloged in Geisler-Howe and Archer, is that the Greek verbs differ: Mark uses *airō* ("take along") for the staff, while Matthew uses *ktaomai* ("acquire/procure") — so Jesus was telling them not to *acquire* a new staff while permitting one they already had. This works for the staff. It doesn't work for the sandals: Matthew 10:10 explicitly says *mēde hypodēmata* ("nor sandals") in the list of things not to procure, while Mark 6:9 says *alla hypodedemenous sandalia* ("but having sandals bound on") — a present-tense participle describing their *current* state of being shod. The two passages describe incompatible departure conditions, not the same scene with different verbs. Critical scholarship (Davies-Allison, Marcus, Fitzmyer) reads the variation as redactional intensification — Matthew and Luke ratchet up the radical poverty of the mission charge to match the prophetic-charismatic ideal of their communities. The harmonization rescues the staff at best; the sandals are still a direct contradiction. That is of course a textual judgment, but the Greek participle is doing the work.

commentary_out.commentary:
The packing instructions for the disciples' mission are the textbook Synoptic-problem contradiction, and they are among the clearest demonstrations that the evangelists edited their sources rather than transcribed them. Mark, the earliest Gospel, has Jesus permit two items: "that they should take nothing for their journey, save a staff only (ei mē rhabdon monon)... but be shod with sandals (alla hypodedemenous sandalia)" (Mark 6:8-9). Matthew prohibits both: in the list of things not to provide he includes "neither shoes, nor yet staves (mēde hypodēmata mēde rhabdon)" (Matt 10:10). Luke 9:3 likewise forbids a staff ("neither staves"), and Luke 10:4, in the sending of the seventy, adds "carry... no shoes." Mark equips the missionaries with a staff and sandals; Matthew and Luke strip both away.

The directionality is significant. On the two-source hypothesis, where Matthew and Luke independently agree against Mark, source critics look for a shared cause. Here that cause is most plausibly the Q mission discourse, which transmitted a stricter, more radical form of the charge reflecting the wandering-charismatic ideal of voluntary destitution current in the communities behind Q. Matthew and Luke conflated Mark's instruction with the Q version and produced the more rigorous prohibition.

The apologetic harmonization, catalogued in Geisler and Howe and in Archer, leans on a lexical distinction in the verbs. Mark uses airō ("to take up, carry along") of the staff, whereas Matthew's list is governed by ktaomai ("to acquire, procure") — the prohibition opens at Matthew 10:9 with mē ktēsēsthe ("do not acquire"), and the staff, sandals, and the rest in 10:10 hang off that verb as its objects. So, the argument runs, Mark permits carrying a staff one already owns while Matthew forbids procuring a new one. Give the harmonizer his due, and give him the whole list: under the ktaomai reading the ban covers the sandals exactly as it covers the staff, since hypodēmata in 10:10 is just another thing not to procure. The move is internally consistent for Matthew on its own terms — it does not split apart on the sandals the way one might assume. The strongest form of the harmonization rescues Matthew across the board.

The trouble is that it cannot touch Luke or Mark, and that is where the contradiction actually lives. Luke 9:3 does not use ktaomai at all — it uses airete (present imperative of airō, "take"), the same carry-it-along verb Mark uses, and still forbids the staff outright (mēte rhabdon). There is no "acquire versus carry" wiggle room in Luke; the disciples are told to take nothing, and Luke 10:4 adds "no shoes" to the seventy. And Mark is not describing a future acquisition either. Mark 6:9 has the disciples already shod as they leave — hypodedemenous sandalia, a perfect middle participle of hypodeō (hypodeomai) describing their settled state of being bound into their sandals at the moment of departure. Set Mark beside Luke and the verb-distinction evaporates: Mark sends them out wearing sandals and carrying a staff; Luke sends them out (airō) forbidden to take either. That is a flat contradiction in departure conditions, and no "having versus acquiring" distinction reaches it, because both Mark and Luke are talking about what the missionaries leave with, not what they procure on the road.

Critical scholarship (Davies and Allison; Marcus; Fitzmyer; Hagner; Luz) reads the divergence as redactional intensification. Mark's relatively practical provision — a staff for the road and sandals for the feet, but no money, bread, or spare tunic — is sharpened by Matthew and Luke into a more austere image of the missionary, stripped even of the traveler's basic gear and wholly dependent on his hosts. The radicalization fits the prophetic-charismatic self-understanding of the communities that preserved the Q form of the charge. The airō/ktaomai distinction may save Matthew on its own terms, but that internal rescue buys the harmonizer nothing, because the contradiction is between Gospels, not inside one. Verdict: genuine contradiction arising from redactional intensification of Mark via Q — locatable squarely in the Mark–Luke clash, which the verb-distinction cannot reach.

commentary_out.change_summary: Corrected the morphology of hypodedemenous (Mark 6:9) from the inaccurate 'perfect/aorist participle' to a perfect middle participle of hypodeō/hypodeomai describing the disciples' state of being already shod at departure. Reframed the airō/ktaomai harmonization per audit: clarified that Matthew's mē ktēsēsthe (10:9) governs both staff and sandals, so the ktaomai reading is internally consistent for Matthew and does not 'collapse' on the sandals; relocated the genuine contradiction to the Mark–Luke clash (Mark depart shod + staff; Luke uses airō and forbids both), which the verb-distinction cannot touch. Verdict and length preserved.
